explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, "I have given the beloved of My soul into the hands of her enemies." (Jeremiah 12:7) Notice He calls her the beloved of His soul, and the very next thing is that heavy handing over. I think this is a hard verse to read out loud, so take your time with it.

Priests are a good guess, friend, since they're all over this book. But the verse says the beloved of His soul is given into the hands of her enemies. (Jeremiah 12:7) That word enemies is the one to hold onto. It sounds heavy because it is.

Kings sound official, I'll give you that. But the LORD says He has given the beloved of His soul "into the hands of her enemies." (Jeremiah 12:7) Nobody here is handed over to a throne. The verse says enemies, plain and simple.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, "She has roared against Me." (Jeremiah 12:8) A lion in the forest doesn't whisper, and this one is roaring at Him. That's the picture He chose, so we keep it just like that.

Running away is what I'd do around a real lion, baker. But the verse says the opposite: "She has roared against Me." (Jeremiah 12:8) This lion isn't sneaking off anywhere. It's making noise, and it's pointed at Him.

Hiding is a quiet move, friend, and this verse is anything but quiet. The LORD says His inheritance is like a lion in the forest, and "She has roared against Me." (Jeremiah 12:8) A roaring lion isn't hiding behind a tree. Keep that sound in your head.

I get the thought, baker, but it's the other way around. The LORD describes a speckled bird of prey with "other birds of prey circling against her." (Jeremiah 12:9) Circling against her, not around her to guard her. If you're a bird and a whole flock of birds of prey is circling, that's not a welcome party.

Right, friend. The text says the other birds of prey are "circling against her." (Jeremiah 12:9) They aren't there to protect the speckled bird. It's a picture of a bird with trouble circling overhead.

explanations.answer: All the beasts of the field
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD says, "Go, gather all the beasts of the field; bring them to devour her." (Jeremiah 12:9) All of them, every beast in the field. I'd be nervous just reading that list.

explanations.answer: All the kings of the earth
explanations.explanation: Kings are a fair guess in a book full of them, friend. But in this verse the command is, "Go, gather all the beasts of the field; bring them to devour her." (Jeremiah 12:9) The word is beasts, not kings. Hold onto the field and the beasts.

explanations.answer: All the families of the north
explanations.explanation: The north does show up in this book, baker. Jeremiah 1:15 mentions the families of the northern kingdoms. But here the command is to gather "all the beasts of the field." (Jeremiah 12:9) Different verse, different gathering.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, "Many shepherds have destroyed My vineyard; they have trampled My plot of ground." (Jeremiah 12:10) Shepherds are supposed to look after things, so that line stings. Many of them, and the plot got trampled.

Good thinking, friend. Little foxes ruin the vineyards in Song of Songs 2:15. But this verse names a different culprit: "Many shepherds have destroyed My vineyard." (Jeremiah 12:10) Foxes are in another book.

A boar can wreck a vineyard, baker. Psalm 80:13 pictures a boar from the forest ravaging a vine. But here the LORD says, "Many shepherds have destroyed My vineyard." (Jeremiah 12:10) That's many, not one.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, "All the land is laid waste, but no man takes it to heart." (Jeremiah 12:11) The land is mourning and nobody takes it to heart. I think that's the sad part, so let it sit a second.

It's true, baker, and I wish it weren't. The verse says, "All the land is laid waste, but no man takes it to heart." (Jeremiah 12:11) So the land lies waste, and the verse says no man takes it to heart. Some verses just need a quiet moment.

That's it, baker. The verse says "the sword of the LORD devours from one end of the earth to the other." (Jeremiah 12:12) It's His sword, and it reaches from one end to the other. Then comes the line, "No flesh has peace."

Nations is a sensible guess, friend. But the verse says "the sword of the LORD devours from one end of the earth to the other." (Jeremiah 12:12) The sword belongs to the LORD, and that's the word to remember.

North would make sense because it shows up elsewhere in Jeremiah, baker. But in this verse it's "the sword of the LORD" that devours "from one end of the earth to the other." (Jeremiah 12:12) That covers a whole lot more than one direction.

Yes, friend. The verse says, "Bear the shame of your harvest because of the fierce anger of the LORD." (Jeremiah 12:13) It's tied right to the thorns they harvested after sowing wheat. That's the only reason the verse gives, so we stick with it.

A dry season would explain a bad harvest, baker. But the verse doesn't say that. It says, "Bear the shame of your harvest because of the fierce anger of the LORD." (Jeremiah 12:13) We stay with what it says.

Locusts are a classic harvest wrecker, friend, but they aren't named here. The verse says, "Bear the shame of your harvest because of the fierce anger of the LORD." (Jeremiah 12:13) Nothing in these verses mentions a single locust.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, "I am about to uproot them from their land." (Jeremiah 12:14) These are the evil neighbors who attack the inheritance He bequeathed to His people Israel. Uproot is the word, so remember it.
Serving Judah sounds like a plan, friend, but the verse never says it. The LORD says, "I am about to uproot them from their land." (Jeremiah 12:14) The word is uproot, not serve.

Handing over their land is a neat idea, baker, but the verse says something else. The LORD says, "I am about to uproot them from their land." (Jeremiah 12:14) It doesn't say who gets the land. We don't add what it leaves out.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, "…and I will uproot the house of Judah from among them." (Jeremiah 12:14) So it's the neighbors, and Judah is uprooted from among them too. It's a heavy line, and it's right there in the text.

I see why you'd think so, baker, but the text says it plainly. The LORD says, "…and I will uproot the house of Judah from among them." (Jeremiah 12:14) Judah is uprooted from among the neighbors too. Good thing the very next verses keep going.

I'm glad you stopped to check, baker, because the text says the opposite. The LORD says, "I will once again have compassion on them." (Jeremiah 12:15) After the uprooting comes compassion again. Never is not in this verse.

Right, friend. After the uprooting, the LORD says, "I will once again have compassion on them and return each one to his inheritance and to his land." (Jeremiah 12:15) So the verse says compassion again, not never. That's a good sentence to carry out of the passage.
Yes, baker. The LORD says He will "return each one to his inheritance and to his land." (Jeremiah 12:15) Each one, to his own land. That's a hopeful line after all that uprooting.

A camp is a fine place to land, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The LORD says He will "return each one to his inheritance and to his land." (Jeremiah 12:15) The word is land. Each one goes back to his own.
A tent would at least be cozy, baker, but the verse names something bigger. The LORD says He will "return each one to his inheritance and to his land." (Jeremiah 12:15) Land is the word we need.

That's right, friend. The LORD says the neighbors once taught His people to swear by Baal, a false god. (Jeremiah 12:16) Now He says they can learn to swear by His name, saying, "As surely as the LORD lives." The same people who taught the wrong oath are invited to learn the right one.

Dagon was a Philistine god (1 Samuel 5:2), so it's a reasonable guess, baker. But the LORD says they taught His people to swear by Baal. (Jeremiah 12:16) The verse puts Baal on the table, and that's the name to remember.

Molech is another false god (Leviticus 18:21), so I see where you were going, friend. But the LORD says the neighbors taught His people to swear by Baal. (Jeremiah 12:16) That's the name in this verse.

explanations.answer: They will be established among His people
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, "then they will be established among My people." (Jeremiah 12:16) The neighbors have to learn the ways of His people and swear by His name first. After that comes the welcome.

explanations.answer: They will be made rulers over His people
explanations.explanation: Rulers is a big leap, friend, and the text doesn't take it. The LORD says, "then they will be established among My people." (Jeremiah 12:16) Established among His people, nothing about ruling.

explanations.answer: They will be kept as His people's servants
explanations.explanation: That's a different promise than the one in the text, baker. The LORD says, "then they will be established among My people." (Jeremiah 12:16) The verse says nothing about servants, only being established among them.

That's the word, friend. The LORD says, "But if they will not obey, then I will uproot that nation; I will uproot it and destroy it, declares the LORD." (Jeremiah 12:17) It's the other side of the if from verse 16. These are the closing words of the message, so they land hard.
Praying is a good thing, baker, but it isn't the word here. The LORD says, "But if they will not obey, then I will uproot that nation." (Jeremiah 12:17) The word is obey.

Fasting turns up in other places in the Bible, friend, but not in this verse. The LORD says, "But if they will not obey, then I will uproot that nation; I will uproot it and destroy it, declares the LORD." (Jeremiah 12:17) The word we want is obey.
